Question: Is this repository actively maintained?
Why is this important?: I don't want to start using something that is a dead-end burden.
Rationale/Source: Recency/frequency signal — last-pushed date, commit cadence — answerable from GitHub API metadata alone (RE's HealthSurveyor), no zipball needed.
Answering Analysis: repository_health + foss_scorecard [checks: foss_scorecard:maintained]

Question: What is this resource, and what is it for?
Why is this important?: Need to understand it to use it appropriately.
Rationale/Source: Purpose/description — from the repo's own GitHub description field, no deeper analysis required.
Answering Analysis: N/A — direct field (Project.description) This might also be a summary of the top level README.

Question: Who owns this resource (accountable owner), and who administers it?
Why is this important?: Are they reputable?
Rationale/Source: repository_health alone answers 'is it maintained', not 'by whom' — the two questions returned the same text until chaoss_metrics, built on project_commits, gave this one its own source.
Answering Analysis: repository_health + chaoss_metrics (contributor identities and concentration)

Question: How widely adopted and active is the community around this repository?
Why is this important?: Reduces adoption risk, provides a health proxy, and ensures community support and responsiveness.
Rationale/Source: Stars are attention, not community. community_support reports the dimensions separately and names the weakest rather than averaging, so 'popular but unsupported' stays visible instead of averaging out.
Answering Analysis: repository_health + community_support (attention, participation and channels as separate dimensions, weakest named) + chaoss_metrics

Why is this important?: Has someone already done this analysis? What did they learn?
Rationale/Source: "Known inventory" check — is there already a catalog asset for this repo, independent of whether it's registered in Resource Explorer's own local registry. Ties to the Scouting "shop for data" search work.
Answering Analysis: N/A — direct field (is_published/egeria_asset_guid); GAP: known-inventory search across the Egeria catalog itself isn't built (Scouting's "shop for data" Track 1)

Question: What explicit licence does this resource use, and are there non-standard or copyleft terms?
Why is this important?: Identifies strict copyleft (GPL/AGPL), source-available shifts (BSL/SSPL), or dual-licensing risks before code integration.
Rationale/Source: GitHub API license field gives the SPDX id cheaply (Scouting); license_classification (Assessment) categorizes it into a risk tier (permissive/weak copyleft/strong copyleft/source-available/unknown) — candidate reference tools for deeper provenance: FOSSology (Linux Foundation compliance workspace), LicenseFinder, ClearlyDefined (crowdsourced licensing/provenance data), Mend, Black Duck. SPDX (ISO/IEC 5962) is the standard schema this conforms to.
Answering Analysis: license_classification [checks: license_classification:license_risk_tier]

Question: Is intellectual property (IP) provenance managed via CLA or DCO?
Why is this important?: Protects the organization from copyright infringement claims from unauthorized third-party contributions.

Why is this important?: Prevents unauthorized leakage of internal network metadata, system details, or usage patterns.
Rationale/Source: Matches known telemetry and analytics SDK imports and endpoints in source, and separately checks whether each match is disclosed in the repo's own docs. An undisclosed match is the finding, not the presence of telemetry.
Answering Analysis: telemetry_scan

Question: For AI/ML assets, what licensing or usage constraints apply to models, weights, or datasets?

Question: How does the repository handle secrets, credentials, and sensitive configurations?
Why is this important?: Prevents hardcoded secrets or unencrypted credential passing in containerized and automated deployment environments.
Rationale/Source: Runs a vendored gitleaks ruleset over the HEAD snapshot of tracked files, naming the ruleset and commit. Never claims 'no secrets' — only 'no matches against this ruleset, in this snapshot' — and says nothing about git history, where a removed secret still lives.
Answering Analysis: secret_scan

Question: How concentrated is authorship — would the project survive losing its top contributors?

Rationale/Source: chaoss_metrics reports the elephant factor and related CHAOSS metrics on their own terms, never averaged into a score. No question referenced it.
Answering Analysis: chaoss_metrics

Question: How much code is there? How complex?
Why is this important?: Gives an estimate on cost to maintain.
Rationale/Source: Both halves are answerable as of 2026-09-02. SIZE: language_file_classification carries a per-language line census — code, comment, docstring and blank — written at ingestion and at Coarse Profile refresh (pipeline.py::_record_line_census). Markdown, JSON, HTML, CSS, SQL and XML are counted as text and excluded from the code total by construction; project_stats.ingestion_lines_of_code, which counted every newline in every text file and reported 1,118,195 against ~156k real code lines on egeria-python, is retired and must not be cited. COMPLEXITY: api_structure carries the per-language max/mean it always computed, python and java only — go and javascript store 0 for every symbol because their extractors never compute it, so they are excluded and named rather than averaged in (0.32 vs 2.69 on milvus). A repo with no census reports no line counts rather than zero: not counted is not the same as no code.
Answering Analysis: language_file_classification + api_structure

Question: What are the public interfaces?
Why is this important?: How do we use this - does it look like it does what we want?

(api_structure + interface_surface).
Answering Analysis: interface_surface

Question: Can Egeria's survey engine reach this resource, or must Resource Explorer survey it locally — and which is cheaper?
Why is this important?: Whether a survey can run at all, and where it runs, decides the cost and the provenance of every answer that follows.
Rationale/Source: Reachability is testable by running the native survey with finalAnalysisStep=CHECK_ASSET from the engine host; efficiency is a separate axis (data locality, latency to first result, load on the source, concurrency, provenance) — see multi-resource-questions-design.md §3 rule B. An unreachable resource falls back to a Resource Explorer local mirror published under the native annotation shapes, plus an RFA recording that Egeria could not reach it.
Answering Analysis: GAP: no reachability probe exists — this needs a CHECK_ASSET-only engine action plus the observed-cost comparison step_cost_observer already collects.

Question: Where is this resource physically located, under which jurisdiction, and are there residency or transfer constraints?
Why is this important?: Data sovereignty decides whether we may hold or process this at all, independently of what the licence permits.
Rationale/Source: Two halves. The machine half reads host and region from the connection endpoint, cloud instance metadata, or the mount and file path. The human half — legal controller, residency rule — comes through Enrichment. The result is published as a proposed Egeria DataScope classification carrying scopeElements {jurisdiction, region, controller}.
Answering Analysis: GAP: nothing populates DataScope from a survey today; endpoint geolocation and the Enrichment section are both unbuilt.

Question: What is the scope of the data in time — collection period, validity and coverage?
Why is this important?: A consumer needs to know which period the data actually covers before trusting any answer drawn from it.
Rationale/Source: The other half of DataScope, and machine-proposable for most types: minimum and maximum of date columns for a database, modification-time range and in-file date ranges for a filesystem, DCAT temporal for a published dataset. Human confirmation of validity and coverage comes through Enrichment.
Answering Analysis: GAP: date-range extraction feeds no DataScope proposal today, and the column-level profiling that would supply the ranges is itself unbuilt.

Question: Are there any restrictions for use beyond the licence — classification, zone or terms of use?
Why is this important?: A permissive licence does not mean an internal classification, a governance zone or a contractual term allows the use I have in mind.
Rationale/Source: Separated from the licence question itself when that one became cross-type and moved to Scouting. Reads Egeria governance zones and classifications, the resource's own terms-of-use text, and Enrichment for anything contractual that is not written down machine-readably.
Answering Analysis: GAP: zone and classification restrictions are not read back into the question layer, and agent interpretation of non-standard terms is unbuilt.

Question: Is this resource ready to be offered as a data product — owner, description, licence or agreement, schema, freshness, contact and scope?
Why is this important?: The supply half of a data product: one with no accountable owner, no licence and no stated scope cannot responsibly be offered.
Rationale/Source: A composite over facts other questions already establish — Egeria Ownership, a description, License or DataSharingAgreement, a schema, freshness signals, a contact and a DataScope. Design §4 requires this and the demand question to hold together before a DigitalProduct is proposed.
Answering Analysis: GAP: no readiness composite exists, and several of its inputs (DataScope, agreement, freshness) are themselves gaps.

Question: Is there a defined need or market for this resource — subscriptions, requests, existing use, feedback or open requests for this kind of data?
Why is this important?: The demand half: building a data product nobody asked for costs more than it returns.
Rationale/Source: Reads Egeria DigitalSubscription, Resource Explorer's own registry of existing use and feedback, similar-resource search hits, and open RFAs asking for this kind of data. Design §4 requires this and the readiness question to hold together before a DigitalProduct is proposed.
Answering Analysis: GAP: DigitalSubscription is not read, and RFAs are not searchable by the kind of data they ask for.

Question: How big is this database — schemas, tables, views, columns, rows and bytes?
Why is this important?: Size sets the cost of every later tier, and is the first thing that says whether this is a toy or a production estate.
Rationale/Source: Whole-database catalog reads only, no row data: information_schema and pg_catalog give the structural counts, and relation sizes plus row counts give the volume. Design §5.1 — extract everything the catalog already knows before reading a row.
Answering Analysis: MIXED: schema_inventory (structural counts) + row_count_snapshot (rows and bytes)

Question: Which schemas carry the data, and which are system, empty or staging?
Why is this important?: Knowing which schemas matter stops every later analysis from paying to profile scratch and system objects.
Rationale/Source: Derived from the same catalog read as the size question — object counts and sizes per schema, plus name conventions. Cheap, whole-database, no row data.
Answering Analysis: schema_inventory

Question: Is this database alive — writes since the statistics were reset, last vacuum or analyse, and is anything reading it?
Why is this important?: A database nobody writes to and nobody reads is a retirement candidate, not a survey candidate.
Rationale/Source: pg_stat_user_tables carries n_tup_ins/upd/del, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum/autovacuum/analyze, seq_scan and idx_scan; pg_stat_database carries the transaction and block counters. All of it is a catalog read. Note the two absence modes design §5.1 calls out: a counter the engine does not support is not_established, and statistics that were never collected must render as "run ANALYZE", not as "no activity".
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_activity_signals (proposed) — the tuple and scan counters are not read by any analysis today.

Question: Is this database documented — what fraction of its tables and columns carry comments?
Why is this important?: Undocumented tables are the single biggest obstacle to anyone reusing a database they did not build.
Rationale/Source: pg_description via obj_description and col_description gives comments per table and per column; the measure is coverage, not presence. Note rule 13 in the package CLAUDE.md — these need the schema-qualified (schema.table)::regclass form.
Answering Analysis: GAP: nothing measures comment coverage across a database's tables and columns. Design §5.2 proposes a new database comment-coverage analysis; its proposed id is deliberately not spelled out in this note, because it contains a readable repo analysis id as a substring and the stale-gap guard matches on substrings.

Question: What engine and version is this, which extensions are installed, and is the version still supported?
Why is this important?: An unsupported engine version is a security and upgrade liability before anything about the data matters.
Rationale/Source: Server-level rather than database-level — design §5 makes server, database, schema and table each addressable, and this row belongs to the server subset. Sources: version(), pg_settings, pg_extension, and the upstream support window for the major version.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_server_profile (proposed, server-level) — no analysis reads pg_settings, pg_extension or the version support window.

Question: Is this database a primary or a replica, is it clustered, and is WAL archiving or backup configured?
Why is this important?: Whether the data survives a failure is a property of the deployment, not of the schema, and nothing else in a survey reveals it.
Rationale/Source: Catalog-observable: pg_is_in_recovery() for the primary/standby role, pg_stat_replication for standbys and replay lag, pg_settings.archive_mode with pg_stat_archiver for WAL archiving, pg_extension and roles for backup tooling such as pgBackRest, barman or wal-g, Citus catalogs for clustering. Design §5.5 — last successful backup and tested restore are NOT observable and are asked separately.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_resilience (proposed) — none of the replication, archiving or clustering catalog reads exists today.

Question: When was this database last backed up successfully, and has a restore ever been tested?
Why is this important?: These are the two resilience questions a data owner actually asks, and the two that nothing inside the database can answer.
Rationale/Source: Design §5.5 draws the line explicitly: primary/standby role, replicas, WAL archiving and extension-based backup tooling are catalog-observable, while last successful backup, tested restore and RPO/RTO are not. They come from an Enrichment "Backup and recovery" section, and the answer envelope must say which half answered.
Answering Analysis: N/A — human-supplied via the Enrichment Context form (the Enrichment half of the proposed db_resilience analysis).

Question: What kind of database is this — transactional, analytical, reference data, staging or a copy?
Why is this important?: The kind of database decides which later analyses are worth paying for at all.
Rationale/Source: Zero new fetch — reasons over what Scouting already stored: table shapes, foreign-key density, naming conventions, read/write ratios from the tuple counters, and the query mix if pg_stat_statements is installed.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_classification (proposed) — the inputs are all available and nothing derives a classification from them.

Question: Is there a data model here — do the tables relate through foreign keys, or is this a bag of tables?
Why is this important?: A database with no declared relationships needs a very different kind of attention from one with a real model.
Rationale/Source: Zero new fetch: the foreign-key constraints Scouting already read become a graph, and the measure is connectivity — orphan tables, components, in-degree.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_relationship_graph (proposed) — schema_inventory records the constraints but builds no graph from them.

Question: What is the grain of each table — one row per what?
Why is this important?: Grain is the first thing a consumer has to know and the last thing most databases write down.
Rationale/Source: Inferred from primary-key composition, column names, n_distinct approaching the row count, and date columns — emitted as an Egeria DataGrainAnnotation with a grainStatement and a confidence. Shared with the filesystem path, where the same inference runs over a data file's columns.
Answering Analysis: GAP: grain_determination (proposed) — Egeria's DataGrain and DataGrainAnnotation types exist, but no service or analysis populates them.

Question: Does this look like a copy or a subset of a database we already know?
Why is this important?: Paying to survey, host and govern the third copy of the same database is a cost nobody decided to take on.
Rationale/Source: A schema signature — table and column names, types, key structure — hashed into a fingerprint and compared against the fingerprints of databases already in the registry. Egeria's FingerprintAnnotation is the publication shape.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_fingerprint (proposed) — FingerprintAnnotation exists as a type; no signature is computed or compared.
Answering Mechanism: Database Catalog Query + Local Registry Query

Question: Are there views, materialised views, functions or triggers that encode business logic?
Why is this important?: Logic hidden in views and triggers is logic no application-level survey will ever find.
Rationale/Source: The DDL is already in the catalog (pg_views, pg_matviews, pg_proc, pg_trigger) and Resource Explorer already parses view DDL with SQLGlot for dependencies, column lineage and complexity. What is missing is the link from that step's output back to the question layer.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: the sql_analysis survey step parses view DDL with SQLGlot, but it is a survey step only — analysis_catalog.yaml has no sql_analysis entry, so nothing in the question layer resolves its result.

Question: Which tables would a consumer start with?
Why is this important?: A hundred-table database with no entry point is functionally undiscoverable, however well it is catalogued.
Rationale/Source: A ranking rather than a measure: foreign-key in-degree, row counts, presence of comments and read activity from the scan counters, combined into a short starting list. Zero new fetch.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_hub_tables (proposed) — every input exists; nothing combines them into a ranking.

Question: Which columns hold semi-structured data (JSON, JSONB, XML, arrays or hstore), and how much of the data sits in them?
Why is this important?: Data hidden inside JSON columns is invisible to every schema-level question, and is often where the interesting fields live.
Rationale/Source: Zero new fetch — the column types are already in the catalog read; what is derived is which columns are semi-structured and what share of the stored bytes they account for. The contents themselves are a separate, more expensive Analysis question.
Answering Analysis: GAP: schema_inventory records the column types but derives no semi-structured-column check from them.

Question: What is the full schema — tables, columns, types, keys, constraints and indexes?
Why is this important?: The schema is the contract, and every structural question downstream is asked against it.
Rationale/Source: The complete catalog read: information_schema and pg_catalog for schemas, tables, columns and types; pg_constraint for primary, foreign, unique and check constraints; pg_index for indexes. Published under Egeria's own Relational* metric keys so a native and a local run are comparable (design §2.2).
Answering Analysis: schema_inventory

Question: What do the columns actually contain — nulls, distinct counts, most-common values, ranges and widths?
Why is this important?: Types say what a column may hold; only the values say what it does hold.
Rationale/Source: pg_stats, populated by ANALYZE, already carries null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds, avg_width and correlation — column profiling with no sampling at all. Value sampling is the fallback for columns whose statistics are stale or missing. Design §5.8: the answer envelope must state which route ran and, when sampled, the strategy, bound and seed.
Answering Analysis: GAP: column_profile (proposed) — pg_stats is never read, and no sampling fallback exists.

Question: Which columns conform to a known Data Class, with what confidence, and which look like a class we do not have yet?
Why is this important?: Knowing where the sensitive data actually sits is the precondition for every privacy and access question after it.
Rationale/Source: Generalises the existing PII matching: column name, type and sampled value patterns matched against every Egeria DataClass, producing a DataClassAnnotation per column with a stated confidence. Columns that show a clear pattern but match nothing raise an RFA proposing a new Data Class, carrying the observed pattern. Per design §5.8 the confidence is always stated against the sample, never as an unqualified "conforms".
Answering Analysis: GAP: data_class_match (proposed) — today's matching runs over view-lineage leaf columns only, never base tables, and no RFA proposes a new class.

Question: Which low-cardinality columns conform to a known reference-data set, and which should become one?
Why is this important?: Uncontrolled code columns are where data quality quietly fails, and they are cheap to find.
Rationale/Source: Columns whose n_distinct falls under a threshold have their distinct values compared against every Egeria ValidValueSet. A full match becomes ValidValuesAssignment advice; a partial match raises an RFA listing the unmatched values; no match at all raises an RFA proposing a new ValidValueSet carrying the values.
Answering Analysis: GAP: reference_data_match (proposed) — nothing compares distinct values against ValidValueSets or proposes a new set.

Question: What is inside the JSON, JSONB and XML columns — keys, nesting, types, and consistency across rows?
Why is this important?: A schema that stops at "jsonb" describes the column and says nothing about the data.
Rationale/Source: JSONB via jsonb_object_keys and jsonb_typeof over a bounded sample, giving key frequency, nesting depth and type consistency across rows; XML via the root element and xpath key sampling. The result is a SchemaAnalysisAnnotation carrying an inferred nested schema, sharing its inference core with the filesystem path's JSON and XML file profiling.
Answering Analysis: GAP: nested_column_profile (proposed) — semi-structured column contents are never sampled or shape-inferred.

Question: Which tables have no primary key, no foreign key, no comment, unused indexes, or names that break the convention?
Why is this important?: These are the specific, fixable defects behind a vague sense that a database is badly kept.
Rationale/Source: Check-granular in the same shape as the repository conventions analysis: each defect is its own named check so an assessment can cite it and a subscription can watch it. All of it reads the catalog, including pg_stat_user_indexes for indexes nothing uses.
Answering Analysis: GAP: schema_conventions (proposed) — none of these checks exists for databases.

Question: What does this database depend on outside itself — foreign data wrappers, dblink, extensions or publications?
Why is this important?: An external dependency is a reachability, security and upgrade constraint that the schema alone never shows.
Rationale/Source: pg_foreign_server and pg_foreign_table for FDWs, pg_extension for extensions including dblink, pg_publication and pg_subscription for logical replication. A catalog read, no row data.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_external_dependencies (proposed) — none of these catalogs is read today.

Question: Who can read and write what — roles, grants, superusers, PUBLIC grants, and are sensitive columns readable broadly?
Why is this important?: Access is only half an answer; access crossed with sensitivity is the half anyone acts on.
Rationale/Source: pg_roles, role_table_grants and pg_default_acl give the access half and already have an analysis. The sensitivity half needs column-level Data Class matching, and the question is the cross of the two — which is why a broad PUBLIC grant on an unremarkable table and the same grant on a table of personal data read identically today.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: privilege_audit answers the roles, grants, superuser and PUBLIC-grant half; the sensitive-column half needs the proposed data_class_match and the join between the two, neither of which is built.

Question: How is this database changing — rows inserted, updated and deleted per table per period, size drift and schema churn?
Why is this important?: A point-in-time survey cannot distinguish a busy table from an abandoned one; the deltas can.
Rationale/Source: Deltas of the n_tup_ins/upd/del counters and of relation sizes between two stored snapshots, per table, producing a series the Understanding tier can chart and the change detectors in design §9 can threshold. Depends on the structured per-snapshot tables, not on re-parsing the survey JSON blob.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_change_rates (proposed) — row_count_snapshot records a point in time and nothing derives a delta series between snapshots.

Question: Which glossary terms do these columns probably mean?
Why is this important?: Columns bound to agreed terms are the difference between a catalogued database and an understandable one.
Rationale/Source: Suggestions rather than assignments, drawn from column names, any matched Data Classes and any matched reference-data sets, and published as Egeria SemanticAnnotations for a steward to accept or reject.
Answering Analysis: GAP: semantic_suggestions (proposed) — SemanticAnnotation exists as a type and nothing produces one.

Question: How complete and consistent is this database's documentation?
Why is this important?: Documentation coverage is the scored version of the Scouting comment question, and the one a steward is measured on.
Rationale/Source: Scores the coverage measure against criteria and adds the convention checks — a database where every table has a comment but half of them repeat the table name is not well documented.
Answering Analysis: GAP: neither the proposed database comment-coverage measure nor schema_conventions exists yet, so there is nothing to score. See the Scouting comment-coverage row for why the proposed id is not written out here.

Question: What is the sensitive-data exposure — which sensitive columns can which roles read?
Why is this important?: This is the question a privacy review actually asks, and it is a cross of two analyses rather than either one.
Rationale/Source: The scored form of the access-and-sensitivity question in Analysis: sensitive columns identified by Data Class matching, crossed with who holds read access to them, weighted by the breadth of the grant. A PUBLIC grant on a column of personal data is the finding this exists to surface.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: privilege_audit supplies who can read what; the sensitive-column half needs the proposed data_class_match, and nothing crosses the two today.

Question: How well-modelled is this database — keys, constraints, foreign-key coverage, orphan tables and grain clarity?
Why is this important?: Modelling quality predicts how expensive this database will be to integrate with anything else.
Rationale/Source: Scores the convention checks together with grain clarity: a table whose grain cannot be stated is a modelling defect even when its constraints are all present.
Answering Analysis: GAP: schema_conventions and grain_determination are both proposed.

Question: How well-governed is this database's reference data — what share of its low-cardinality columns are bound to a set?
Why is this important?: Reference-data governance is measurable as a share, which makes it one of the few governance claims that can be tracked over time.
Rationale/Source: The denominator is the columns whose cardinality makes them reference-data candidates; the numerator is those bound to an Egeria ValidValueSet. Both come from the reference-data matching analysis.
Answering Analysis: GAP: reference_data_match (proposed) supplies the checks, and nothing measures the bound share.

Question: Is this database maintained and healthy — vacuum recency, dead-tuple ratio and unused indexes?
Why is this important?: Operational neglect shows up in the statistics long before it shows up as an outage.
Rationale/Source: Scores the activity signals against thresholds: how long since the last vacuum or analyse, the ratio of dead to live tuples, and indexes that have never been scanned. Remember design §5.1's absence rule — statistics that were never collected must not read as a healthy zero.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_activity_signals (proposed) — vacuum recency and dead-tuple ratios sit in pg_stat_user_tables and are not read.

Question: Is this database resilient — replica present, archiving on, backup evidence and a tested restore?
Why is this important?: A data owner signing off on a database is signing off on its recovery, not its schema.
Rationale/Source: Design §5.5 makes this deliberately two-sided: the catalog facts (role, replicas, archiving, backup tooling) and the Enrichment facts (last successful backup, tested restore, RPO and RTO). The envelope must say which half answered, because a green score drawn only from the catalog half would claim something nobody verified.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_resilience (proposed) combines catalog facts with an Enrichment "Backup and recovery" section; neither half is built.
